title: A Machine for Jumping to Conclusions
hook: The storm-cell acetate lines up beautifully, and the missing offshore reading disappears from the verdict.
counterintuition: The trap is not speed alone. A thin story can feel complete because WYSIATI treats visible evidence as enough, so the better move is to ask what is absent before confidence hardens.
tryThisNow: Pick one confident judgment from today and write a missing-evidence line under it. Name the fact, view, or record that could change the story.
keyTakeaway: Before a coherent story becomes your verdict, ask what missing information would matter if it were visible.

breakdown.fastRead:
A forecaster sees three storm cells line up neatly on the afternoon map. The pattern says landfall will miss the coast. The story is coherent, and confidence rises with that coherence.

But coherence is not coverage.

WYSIATI means what you see is all there is. The mind forms a story from visible pieces and often forgets the missing ones. The correction is simple and difficult: before the verdict, ask what evidence is absent. A tidy story built from thin evidence should stay provisional until the missing offshore reading, second witness, or base record has been checked.
breakdown.deepRead:
A pediatric triage nurse sees a smiling child with a normal oxygen saturation sticker labeled thin evidence. The visible facts say low concern. The waiting room is full, the chart looks ordinary, and the parent is calm.

The story fits.

That fit is the danger. The mind likes coherence more than completeness. If the available pieces make a clean shape, confidence rises even when the evidence is thin. WYSIATI turns the visible set into the whole world: smile, normal sticker, calm parent, routine code. The absent pieces, recent fever, fluid intake, exposure, breathing pattern before arrival, have no voice because they are not on the table.

Jumping to conclusions is not just haste. It is a feature of a system that needs to make sense quickly. A few aligned cues can produce a strong judgment because there is no internal meter saying, only three of the nine relevant facts have arrived. The mind measures the quality of the story more readily than the quantity of evidence behind it.

A freight dispatch room can show the same failure. The loading-bay placard labeled coherence lists a clean chain of custody, and the receiver's complaint sounds exaggerated. The story says release the truck. Then someone asks which evidence would change the call: scale ticket, seal photo, temperature log. The confidence weakens, not because the first story was absurd, but because the missing information finally becomes visible.

Ask for the absent fact before you admire the story.
breakdown.fullRead:
You can feel a conclusion become solid while the evidence is still thin. A client seems unreliable. A plate looks wrong. A museum object appears authentic. A storm will miss. The story has enough pieces to explain itself, and once it explains itself, the mind stops asking what else should be there.

That is the force of WYSIATI. What you see is all there is. The available evidence forms a coherent story, and the missing evidence is treated less like missing evidence than like nonexistence. The resulting confidence can be impressive because confidence often tracks coherence, not coverage.

What would you ask for if you were not allowed to decide yet?

That question interrupts the machine. It turns the invisible into a checklist. Who has not been heard? Which measurement is absent? What base record is missing? Which rival explanation would need a fact we have not collected? The point is not to gather infinite data. The point is to stop a tidy story from pretending it has no blank spaces.

A museum conservation lab offers a clean example. The pigment swatch folder labeled WYSIATI shows colors that match the claimed period. The frame, label, and surface all agree. It is easy to feel that the object has passed. But the missing check may be binding medium, underdrawing, provenance gap, or restoration history. The visible pieces create coherence; the absent pieces may carry the decision.

A restaurant expo line makes the same mistake in seconds. The ticket rail spike labeled confidence holds three late orders from the same station, and the chef blames the new line cook. The story is tidy: new person, late station, bad pacing. Missing from the story are printer lag, table changes, and a runner who carried two plates to the wrong section. Until those absent facts are named, the confidence is just coherence with a narrow field of view.

This is not a rule to distrust every story. Stories are how scattered facts become usable. The problem appears when the story feels complete because every visible piece fits. If the evidence is thin, fit can be cheap. Two cues can fit perfectly and still omit the fact that would reverse the judgment.

A public defender intake shows the cost. A plea calendar tab labeled missing information says the client missed one prior date, has no stable address, and arrived late today. The conclusion writes itself: unreliable. But the absent evidence is transport, phone access, work schedule, and whether the prior date notice was mailed correctly. If those facts are not gathered, the verdict is not a judgment about the client. It is a judgment about the visible file.

The limit is practical. You cannot ask for every absent fact. The discipline is to ask for the one absent fact that would matter most if it were visible. In medicine, it may be a vital sign. In law, a notice record. In forecasting, an offshore buoy. In hiring, a work sample. In operations, a log that checks the story's weakest link.

A coherent story is allowed to guide attention. It is not allowed to impersonate completeness. Before you conclude, make the missing evidence speak.

planSpec.requiredBeat: the operator places the conclusions storm-cell acetate labeled jumping to conclusions beside the tempting first answer, covers the answer field with a palm, and speaks the correction

examples.scenario: The ridged edge of the conclusions storm-cell acetate labeled jumping to conclusions catches Grace's sleeve as three cells align offshore. The visible map says miss the coast, and the alert field is waiting. She covers the field with her palm and names the blank: no current buoy reading south of the shelf. Grace must decide whether the coherent storm story earns confidence before that absent evidence arrives.
examples.whatToDo: Keep the alert provisional until the missing buoy reading or a substitute offshore measurement is checked against the visible cell pattern.
examples.whyItMatters: The map's coherence creates confidence from what is visible. WYSIATI hides the absent buoy, which may be the fact that changes the forecast.

questions.prompt: A forecaster sees three storm cells aligned in a way that usually misses the coast, but the offshore buoy reading is unavailable. What is the best next move?
choices: Wait for or substitute the missing offshore measurement before treating the story as settled.
Issue the miss forecast because the visible pattern is coherent.
Ignore the storm-cell pattern because any missing data invalidates all visible evidence.
questions.explanation: The visible pattern matters, but WYSIATI hides the absent buoy. Checking or substituting that measurement tests the story. Ignoring the pattern overcorrects; issuing the forecast treats coherence as completeness.

questions.prompt: A museum team sees pigment, label, and frame details that all match a claimed period. Provenance and binding-medium checks are still missing. What risk remains?
choices: The object is probably authentic because independent visible details agree.
The visible matches may create confidence while the missing checks carry the decisive evidence.
The visible evidence should be discarded because missing evidence always dominates.
questions.explanation: Agreement among visible cues creates coherence, not full coverage. The missing provenance and medium checks may reverse the conclusion. The other choices either overtrust the visible set or overdiscard it.

questions.prompt: A freight dispatcher has chain of custody and receiver signature, but no scale ticket or seal photo. The release story feels clean. Which question should come first?
choices: Who sounds more credible, the driver or the receiver?
How quickly can the truck be released without fees?
Which absent record would change the release call if it appeared?
questions.explanation: The missing-record question attacks WYSIATI directly. Credibility and fees may matter later, but they do not test whether the visible story is complete enough for release.

questions.prompt: A child in triage is smiling, has a normal oxygen saturation, and has a calm parent. Fever pattern and fluid intake have not been asked. What is wrong with assigning low priority immediately?
choices: The conclusion is built from a coherent but thin set of visible cues.
Smiling children are always at high risk.
Oxygen saturation is not a useful measure in triage.
questions.explanation: The visible cues fit a low-risk story, but missing history can matter. The other choices make false clinical claims. The actual issue is confidence from thin evidence.

questions.prompt: A restaurant team blames a new cook for three late plates from the grill. Printer lag and runner notes have not been checked. What should the expo do?
choices: Accept the new-cook story because all visible delays point to grill.
Write the blame story, then check process facts that could break it.
Avoid assigning cause because service is too chaotic.
questions.explanation: Writing the story keeps it visible while missing process facts test it. Accepting the story trusts coherence. Avoiding cause gives up on evidence instead of widening the field.

questions.prompt: A public defender sees missed court date, late arrival, and unstable address in a file. Transit, phone access, and notice mailing are unknown. Which judgment is most defensible?
choices: The client is unreliable because all visible facts point that way.
The visible facts should be ignored because poverty explains all attendance issues.
The visible file raises concern, but no-show risk should wait for the missing facts.
questions.explanation: Concern is justified, but the verdict is incomplete without facts that directly affect attendance. Ignoring visible negatives is as sloppy as treating them as the whole person.

questions.prompt: A manager says, "The story is internally consistent, so I am confident." Which reply best targets the reasoning flaw?
choices: Internal consistency can raise confidence even when important evidence is absent.
Internal consistency is useless because only large datasets matter.
Confidence should be avoided in all uncertain decisions.
questions.explanation: The flaw is confusing coherence with completeness. Large datasets and total avoidance of confidence are not the lesson. The key is asking what missing evidence would matter.

questions.prompt: A hiring panel hears a polished story from a candidate and has not checked a work sample or reference. The candidate's answers fit together neatly. What should the panel do?
choices: Advance the candidate because coherent answers predict coherent work.
Ask what evidence is absent from the interview and check the work sample or reference before deciding.
Reject the candidate because polished stories are suspicious.
questions.explanation: The interview story may be useful, but missing evidence outside the story can matter more. Advancing confuses coherence with coverage. Rejecting polish creates the opposite unsupported conclusion.

questions.prompt: An analyst has three customer complaints that all mention the same product feature and concludes the feature is failing. Usage logs and total exposure are missing. What best describes the problem?
choices: Three complaints are never enough to justify any action.
The analyst should trust customer reports over logs because reports contain lived detail.
The complaints form a coherent story, but missing base information may change its meaning.
questions.explanation: The complaints are visible and coherent, but without exposure or usage logs their rate is unknown. The answer is not to ignore complaints or privilege them over records; it is to ask what is absent.

reviewCards.front: A story fits every fact you can see. What should you ask before deciding?
reviewCards.back: Ask what important evidence is absent. Coherence among visible facts is not the same as coverage of the facts that could change the verdict.

reviewCards.front: A file contains only negative facts about a person. What WYSIATI risk appears?
reviewCards.back: The visible file may become the whole person. List missing facts that directly affect the judgment before turning the file into a verdict.

reviewCards.front: A team is confident because three cues point the same way. What is the difference between coherence and coverage?
reviewCards.back: Coherence means the visible cues fit together. Coverage means the relevant evidence set is complete enough. Confidence should depend on coverage, not only fit.

reviewCards.front: How do you make missing information visible in a fast decision?
reviewCards.back: Name the one absent fact that would most change the decision. A single missing-evidence line can stop a tidy story from closing too soon.

reviewCards.front: Why is jumping to conclusions more than simply rushing?
reviewCards.back: Because the mind can build strong confidence from thin evidence when the visible pieces cohere. The error is treating what is visible as all there is.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: The core skill is making absence visible. Before accepting a coherent story, ask which missing fact, witness, measurement, or record would matter most if it appeared.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a recommendation feels coherent after a few visible facts, then write one missing record or view that could change it before approving.
If a case looks routine from visible cues, then ask for the missing symptom, timing, or exposure detail that would make it non-routine.
If a file points cleanly toward one judgment, then list the absent notice, access, or context fact before recommending conditions.
If a story about someone's motive feels complete, then name the missing perspective or fact that could change the interpretation.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, pause on one confident conclusion and add a missing-evidence line. Do not decide until you have named the fact that could change the story.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, review a decision that felt coherent. List visible facts, missing facts, and whether confidence came from fit or coverage.

memorableLines.why: It captures the WYSIATI correction in five words.
It marks the seductive moment before missing evidence is noticed.

memorableLines.text: Before you conclude, make the missing evidence speak.
memorableLines.why: It turns the core move into a direct instruction.
